flawed_step: Proof attempt: (1) Fix eps > 0; we need P(|X_n - X| > eps) -> 0. (2) Bound P(|X_n - X| > eps) using the hypothesis F_{X_n}(t) -> F_X(t). This step cannot be justified. P(|X_n - X| > eps) depends on the joint distribution of (X_n, X), but convergence in distribution only constrains the marginal distribution functions. Marginals do not determine the joint law, so no such bound follows.
counterexample: Let X ~ N(0,1) and X_n = -X for all n. By symmetry F_{X_n} = F_X, so X_n -> X in distribution. But |X_n - X| = 2|X|, so P(|X_n - X| > eps) = P(|X| > eps/2) > 0 for every n. This is a constant and does not go to 0. (A simpler version: X is a fair ±1 coin flip and X_n = -X, which gives P(|X_n - X| > 1) = 1.)
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Convergence in distribution depends only on the marginal laws, while convergence in probability depends on the joint law of X_n and X. The proof fails at the step that tries to control P(|X_n - X| > eps) using only the CDFs. X_n = -X with X symmetric (for example standard normal) is a counterexample. The converse (in probability implies in distribution) is true. The statement would also hold if the limit X were almost surely a constant.
